issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette:
Omar, a 29-year-old train conductor, presented for therapy reporting a state of constant, exhausting watchfulness that had taken over his life in the six months since the incident. He had once taken pride in his work, in the steady rhythm of the trains and the quiet responsibility of his cab. Now, every shift felt like a tightrope walk over a chasm of potential disaster. The event had occurred on a bitterly cold afternoon in late autumn. As he brought his train into the station, a man near the platform edge stumbled, pitching forward into the path of the slowing but still unstoppable train. Omar had a clear, horrifying view of the impact and its immediate, gruesome aftermath. He remembers the specific coldness of the air on his skin as he was forced to exit the cab and stand on the platform, the sight of the man's mangled leg, and the dark, spreading stain of blood on the concrete.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel fundamentally unsafe. The initial shock never fully subsided; instead, it sharpened into a perpetual state of high alert. This sense of imminent threat was most acute when triggered by reminders of that day. The sight of any visible injury on another person, even something as minor as a child's scraped knee or a passenger with a bandaged hand, would cause a jolt of panic to run through him. In those moments, he was certain that another catastrophe was about to unfold. His focus would narrow, and he would immediately begin scanning the platform, his eyes darting between the yellow line and the faces in the crowd, his body braced for a scream or a fall. The sight of blood, whether in a movie or on a news report, had the same effect, sending his heart racing and flooding his mind with the image of the blood-soaked platform.

This constant scanning for danger has become his new baseline. At work, he is superalert, his gaze sweeping the tracks and platforms with an intensity that leaves his eyes dry and his neck aching. His colleagues and supervisors have tried to reassure him, telling him the systems are safe and the odds of another such accident are infinitesimal. Yet, Omar finds it impossible to believe them. Their words feel hollow against the certainty of danger he feels in his gut. He has come to believe that safety is an illusion and that he is the only one vigilant enough to prevent the next tragedy. This profound distrust of safety extends beyond his job. Even at home in his apartment, he cannot relax.

The need to remain on guard has completely eroded his ability to sleep. Lying in bed at night, he feels that closing his eyes would be a dereliction of duty. He listens to every creak of the building, every distant siren, convinced he needs to stay alert for some unspecified threat. The exhaustion is debilitating, leaving him with a persistent tremor in his hands and a fog in his mind that makes his work even more stressful. A few weeks ago, the specific tactile sensation of a cold draft blowing on his forearms in the conductor's cab sent a wave of nausea and terror through him, a stark physical echo of that day on the platform. The experience was so disorienting that he missed a standard radio check-in, earning him a formal warning from his manager. It was this warning, this tangible proof that his internal state was compromising the job he once loved, that finally prompted him to seek help. He is terrified of causing an accident himself, yet even more terrified of letting his guard down for a single second.
